MS COMPUTER SCIENCE · CSULB · RESEARCH PROJECT

Latency & Scalability
of Distributed LLM Inference

A rigorous benchmarking study of a Ray Serve–based LLM inference service on a single CPU machine. Three experiment axes — concurrency, replica scaling, and batching — across 13 runs measuring p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, and failure rate.

WHAT THIS STUDY DEMONSTRATES
FINDING 01
Queueing saturation (M/M/1)
At 25 users, p99 hit 28 seconds — 25× the single-user baseline of 1.1s. Once the CPU runs at full utilization, new requests queue behind running inference jobs. Mean queue length explodes — exactly as Little's Law predicts.
FINDING 02
Replica scaling shows real gains (Amdahl's Law)
1→2 replicas: RPS improved 2.5× (0.8→2.0), p50 dropped from 30s to 13s. 1→4 replicas: peak RPS of 2.2. Unlike GPU systems, CPU context-switching means gains level off — more replicas than cores becomes counterproductive.
FINDING 03
CPU batching: latency-throughput tradeoff
On CPU, batching did not improve throughput as dramatically as on GPU — RPS stayed near 2.0 across all batch sizes. This is a genuine finding: CPU inference is compute-bound per token regardless of batch, unlike GPU matrix parallelism.
FINDING 04
Zero failures across all 13 runs
Ray Serve maintained 100% success rate across 1,380 requests — even at 25 concurrent users with p99 latency exceeding 28 seconds. The system queued and served every request, demonstrating Ray Serve's robust backpressure handling.

💡
Queueing theory in action. At 1 user, p50 is 970ms — pure inference time with no queueing. At 25 users, p50 hits 24,000ms (25×) and p99 reaches 28,000ms. Once the CPU runs at full utilization, every new request queues behind running inference jobs. This is the queueing saturation regime: utilization near 100%, mean queue length explodes (Little's Law), and tail latency becomes extreme — yet Ray Serve served every single request successfully.

💡
Replicas deliver real parallelism — up to a point. 1→2 replicas: RPS improved 2.5× (0.8→2.0 RPS), p50 dropped from 30s to 13s. The second replica lets one inference run while the other handles a new request — true CPU parallelism. 1→4 replicas: peak RPS of 2.2 with p50 at 11s. Gains continue but level off — on a shared CPU, more replicas eventually create context-switching overhead. This is Amdahl's Law: parallelism is bounded by the sequential inference bottleneck.

💡
Key finding: CPU batching does not improve throughput the way GPU batching does. RPS stayed near 2.0 across all batch sizes (1, 4, 8) and wait times. This is a genuine, important result — on CPU, each token is computed sequentially regardless of batch size. Unlike GPU inference where batching fills CUDA cores in parallel, CPU inference is compute-bound per token. The real gain from multiple replicas (0.8→2.2 RPS) was larger than any batching effect — showing that horizontal scaling beats batching on CPU hardware.

HOW TO RUN
QUICK START (PYTHON 3.12)
# 1. Clone and set up environment
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/llm-inference-bench.git
cd llm-inference-bench
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# 2. Install dependencies
pip install -U pip setuptools wheel
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Run all experiments (~30–60 min on CPU)
python python/experiments/run_experiments.py

# 4. Parse results and generate plots
python python/analysis/parse_locust_history.py
python python/analysis/plot_latency.py
python python/analysis/plot_throughput.py

# 5. View this dashboard
open index.html

How this works. Each "request" sends your prompt to Claude through the Anthropic API. Concurrency is simulated by firing N requests at once with Promise.all; batching groups requests into a single combined call, mirroring how Ray Serve's dynamic batching works in the research benchmark. Real network and model latency means your numbers will vary run to run — that's the same noise the original CPU benchmark had to contend with.
